lessons.t: Why places make memory stronger
lessons.intro: You will learn why a familiar place is such a useful memory aid. Linking items to locations gives your brain a ready-made order to follow.

cards.b: Your brain stores spatial layouts with little effort. A room has a natural order, so you can move through it without thinking.
Each item is attached to a spot, so the spot becomes a cue. When you recall the spot, the item comes back with it.
A route you walk often becomes automatic. Start with a place you know well and the technique works from the first attempt.

fig.title: Ordered cues
fig.note: Each spot cues the next item in order.

ex.q: Your route runs hall, kitchen, lounge. You put milk in the hall, eggs in the kitchen and bread in the lounge. If you start at the hall, what do you recall first?
ex.why: You start at the first spot, the hall, and the item placed there is milk. Walking the route in order then brings back eggs and bread.

lessons.tip: Pick a place you could walk through with your eyes closed.

quiz.q: Why does a familiar place help memory?
o: It gives items a fixed order
It removes the need to practise
quiz.why: A familiar layout supplies a built-in sequence of spots for your items.

quiz.q: What makes a spot a good cue?
o: It is easy to picture clearly
quiz.why: A clear, distinct spot is easy to return to and easy to link with an item.

lessons.t: Choosing a route you know by heart
lessons.intro: You will learn how to pick a route for your palace. A route you already know well saves effort and keeps the order clear.

cards.h: Start with a route you use
cards.b: Choose a walk you take most days, such as your home, your street or your office. Familiar routes need little attention, so your effort goes into the items.

cards.h: Count the spots you can name
cards.b: Walk the route in your mind and name each distinct spot. Aim for 10 to 20 spots on a first palace, because a short route is easier to hold.
A route you only half remember will blur when you need it. Pick one you could describe without looking.

fig.title: Spots by room
fig.note: Four rooms can give over twenty spots.

ex.q: Your home route has 3 rooms. Each room has 4 spots along the walls and 2 spots on the furniture. How many spots does the route give you?
ex.why: Each room gives 4 + 2 = 6 spots. Three rooms give 3 x 6 = 18 spots in total.

lessons.tip: Walk the route once in your head before you place anything.

quiz.q: Which route is the best choice for a first palace?
o: A new city you visited once
A map you have never seen
A route you can only half recall
A walk you take most days
quiz.why: Familiar routes need little effort to recall, so your attention goes to the items.

quiz.q: About how many spots suit a first palace?
quiz.why: Ten to twenty spots are enough to hold a short list without becoming hard to walk.

lessons.t: Setting a fixed order of stops
lessons.intro: You will learn how to give your route a fixed order of stops. A stable order means each spot reliably points to the next one.

cards.b: Start at the same door every time so you always know where the route begins. A clear start stops you wondering which spot comes first.
Walk the route in a consistent direction, such as clockwise through your home. A fixed direction makes the next spot predictable.
Once a spot is numbered, keep it in that position. Changing the order later makes old memories point to the wrong item.

fig.title: Fixing the order
fig.note: Repeat the same walk every time you use it.

ex.q: Your route has 8 spots and you place 2 items at each spot. How many items do you hold in total?
ex.why: Each spot holds 2 items, so 8 x 2 = 16 items in total.

lessons.tip: Say the starting point out loud when you begin a walk.

quiz.q: Why fix the direction of a route?
o: It makes each next spot predictable
It means you need fewer spots
It removes the need for images
quiz.why: With a fixed direction, the spot after any given spot is always the same.

quiz.q: What happens if you reorder numbered spots?
o: Old memories point to the wrong items
quiz.why: Earlier memories are tied to positions, so moving them creates confusion.

lessons.t: Doorways as anchor points
lessons.intro: You will learn how doorways and corners make strong anchor points. Clear anchors help you split a route into rooms and keep each group together.

cards.b: Doorways separate one area from the next, so they are natural breakpoints. Placing an item at each threshold tells your brain that a new group starts there.
The corner of a room is a sharp, visible point. Corners make good spots for items you need to recall first.
Choose one kind of spot, such as doors or windows, and stick with it. Consistency makes your route easy to predict.

fig.title: Anchors in a route
fig.note: Doorways and corners give strong anchor spots.

ex.q: A route has 3 rooms. Each room has 1 doorway and 2 corners used as spots. How many anchor spots in total if you use every doorway and corner?
ex.why: Each room gives 1 doorway plus 2 corners, which is 3 spots. Three rooms give 3 x 3 = 9 spots.

lessons.tip: Use the doorway as the first spot in each room.

quiz.q: What makes a doorway a useful anchor?
o: It is a clear change between areas
It can be seen from anywhere
quiz.why: A threshold signals a shift, which helps you group items by room.

quiz.q: Why keep one anchor type across a route?
o: It removes the need to remember
quiz.why: A consistent pattern lets you anticipate the next spot without thinking.

lessons.t: Real routes versus imagined routes
lessons.intro: You will learn when to use a real route and when to design an imagined one. Starting with a real place saves effort, and imagined places can extend your palace later.

cards.b: A place you have lived in already holds many details, like colours and smells. You do not need to invent them, which saves effort.
You can also design a palace that does not exist. It takes more effort, but you control every spot.

cards.h: Mix real and imagined spots later
cards.b: Once real routes feel easy, you can add invented rooms to extend them. Keep the new spots distinct from the old ones.

fig.title: Real versus imagined routes
fig.note: Start with a real route, then build imagined ones later.

ex.q: You build 2 real routes with 12 spots each and 1 imagined route with 6 spots. How many spots are there in total?
ex.why: Add the spots from each route: 12 + 12 + 6 = 30 spots in total.

lessons.tip: Start with a place you can walk through without thinking.

quiz.q: Which route is the easiest to start with?
o: A real route you know well
A map of a foreign city
quiz.why: Known details come for free, so you can focus on placing items.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of imagined routes?
o: They remove the need for images
quiz.why: Because you design them, you can shape each spot to suit your items.

lessons.t: Walking your palace in your head
lessons.intro: You will learn how to walk through your palace in your mind. Repeating the walk turns a loose route into one you can recall reliably.

cards.h: Start with a clear mental picture
cards.b: Close your eyes and picture the first room in full detail. Notice the light, the furniture and where the shadows fall.
Walk from spot to spot, pausing briefly at each one. A steady pace stops you rushing past items you have just placed.
Run through the full palace once a day for a week. Daily walks lock the route into long-term memory.

fig.title: The walk loop
fig.note: Repeat the loop until recall feels effortless.

ex.q: You place 5 items on a route. On your first walk you recall 3, and on the second walk you recall 5. How many more did you recall on the second walk?
ex.why: The gain is 5 minus 3, which is 2 more items recalled on the second walk.

lessons.tip: Walk the route slowly enough that each spot is clearly visible.

quiz.q: What should your first mental picture include?
o: Picturing the room in clear detail
quiz.why: A detailed picture gives you a stable spot to attach each item to.

quiz.q: How often is a daily walk suggested for a week?
quiz.why: Daily walks build long-term recall faster than occasional practice.

lessons.t: Building a palace from your workplace
lessons.intro: You will learn how to build a palace from a place you visit every day. A workplace gives you many distinct objects and a route you already follow.

cards.h: Your desk area is a good start
cards.b: Your workspace is familiar and full of distinct objects. Use the desk, the chair and the nearby shelf as your first spots.
Follow the route you actually take through the office, from entrance to kitchen. Real paths feel natural and are easy to repeat.
Choose spots that are safe to revisit and do not hold private documents. A stable, uncluttered palace is more useful over time.

fig.title: Office route order
fig.note: Walk the same order each day.

ex.q: Your office route has 5 stops. You place 3 items at each stop. How many items are on the route?
ex.why: Five stops with three items each gives 5 x 3 = 15 items.

lessons.tip: Use objects that will not move during the week.

quiz.q: Why is a familiar workplace useful?
quiz.why: Distinct objects give you clear, separate spots for your items.

quiz.q: Which spot is a poor choice?
quiz.why: A private document may change or be sensitive, so it is not a stable anchor.

lessons.t: Adding landmarks inside each room
lessons.intro: You will learn how to split each room into several landmarks. More landmarks give you more spots without making the route longer.

cards.b: A landmark is a distinct feature, such as a sofa, a window or a rug. Several landmarks split a room into clear stops.
Place a single item on each landmark so each spot holds one idea. Crowding items on one landmark makes them blend together.

cards.h: Keep a set order in each room
cards.b: Walk the landmarks in the same order every time, such as left to right. A consistent path keeps the route tidy.

fig.title: Landmarks per room
fig.note: Count the landmarks in each room before you start.

ex.q: A room has 4 landmarks. You place 2 items on each landmark, and you have 3 rooms like this. How many items in total?
ex.why: Each room holds 4 x 2 = 8 items. Three rooms hold 3 x 8 = 24 items.

lessons.tip: Give each landmark a name you can say silently.

quiz.q: Why put only one item on each landmark?
o: Each spot then holds one clear idea
quiz.why: One item per spot keeps each memory distinct and easy to pull out.

quiz.q: What helps a landmark work well?
o: It is distinct and easy to picture
It is shared with another room
quiz.why: A clear, distinct landmark is easy to find again, so it anchors your item reliably.

lessons.t: Testing a route for weak spots
lessons.intro: You will learn how to test your route and find the spots that are not yet clear. Finding weak spots early saves frustration when you need the list.

cards.h: Walk the route with no notes
cards.b: Recall every item in order without looking at your list. Note where you hesitate or forget, since those are your weak spots.
If a spot feels blurry, swap it for a sharper object. Clear anchors reduce the chance of confusion later.

cards.h: Retest until every spot is clear
cards.b: Repeat the walk until each spot brings its item back quickly. Most routes need only two or three test rounds.

fig.title: Test and repair
fig.note: Keep each round short and focused.

ex.q: You test a 10-spot route. On round 1 you recall 6 items, on round 2 you recall 8, and on round 3 you recall 10. How many items did you miss in round 2?
ex.why: Round 2 gave 8 recalls out of 10 spots, so 10 minus 8 means 2 were missed.

lessons.tip: Test your route when you are relaxed, not rushed.

quiz.q: What do you record during a test walk?
quiz.why: Hesitations point to the spots that need a clearer anchor.

quiz.q: How many test rounds does the lesson suggest for most routes?
quiz.why: Two or three rounds are usually enough to make the weak spots clear.

lessons.t: Checking your palace is complete
lessons.intro: You will learn how to check that your palace has enough rooms and spots before you start. A complete count stops you running out of room halfway through a list.

cards.b: List every room and corner in your route before you begin. A complete count prevents you running short halfway through.

cards.h: Check each room has enough spots
cards.b: Make sure each room has at least three clear spots for items. Rooms with only one or two spots are easy to overload.

cards.h: Keep the route ready to reuse
cards.b: Store the full route in your memory and keep the order fixed. A ready route can be reused for any list you need.

fig.title: Rooms in a full palace
fig.note: Every room in the route needs its own clear spots.

ex.q: A palace has 4 rooms, each with 3 clear spots. How many spots are there in total?
ex.why: Four rooms with three spots each give 4 x 3 = 12 spots in total.

lessons.tip: Count your spots out loud once before you start placing items.

quiz.q: Why count the spots before you start?
o: To remove the need for images
quiz.why: A complete count tells you whether the route can hold your full list.

quiz.q: What makes a room hard to use?
o: Having only one or two spots
quiz.why: Few spots force you to crowd items together, which blurs the memories.

lessons.t: Turning abstract words into pictures
lessons.intro: You will learn how to turn abstract words into concrete pictures. Your brain holds objects far more easily than ideas, so a good picture makes the word easy to recall.

cards.b: Your brain holds pictures more easily than ideas. A word like justice is hard to see, so swap it for a concrete object such as a set of scales.

cards.h: Find an object that sounds like it
cards.b: Pick a simple object linked to the word's meaning or sound. Scales can stand for justice because they show balance.

cards.h: Make the picture a real thing
cards.b: Choose an everyday object you could touch. Real objects are easier to imagine than invented creatures.

fig.title: Abstract words versus pictures

pts: Easy to see in your mind

fig.note: Convert every word on your list into a concrete image.

ex.q: You need to remember the word honesty. Which picture is the most concrete?
ex.why: A mirror shows things as they are, so it is concrete and links to honesty.

lessons.tip: If a word is hard to picture, ask what it looks like in use.

quiz.q: What makes a picture easier to remember than a word?
quiz.why: Concrete images match how the brain stores objects and scenes.

quiz.q: Which is a good pick for justice?
quiz.why: Scales show balance, which links directly to fairness and justice.

lessons.t: Why bizarre images stick better
lessons.intro: You will learn why unusual images are easier to remember than ordinary ones. A single odd detail gives your brain something to hold on to.

cards.b: Your brain tags unusual events as worth keeping. An image that breaks normal rules is more likely to be remembered.
Vague strangeness fades quickly, while a precise detail sticks. A cow wearing roller skates is more memorable than a random animal.
Too many strange features compete for attention. Pick one striking twist per item so the image stays clear.

fig.title: From plain to memorable
fig.note: One clear twist turns a plain item into a strong image.

ex.q: A list has 3 items. You give each item one odd detail, and each detail is worth 2 memory points. How many points are there in total?
ex.why: Three items each give 2 points, so 3 x 2 = 6 points in total.

lessons.tip: Make the oddity vivid, not just silly.

quiz.q: Why do unusual images stay in memory?
o: The brain tags them as notable
quiz.why: Unusual events get extra attention, which helps the image store well.

quiz.q: How many odd twists should one image have?
quiz.why: One clear twist keeps the image focused and easy to recall.

lessons.t: Adding motion and action to items
lessons.intro: You will learn how to make items move in your mental pictures. Action turns a static object into a small scene that is easier to recall.

cards.b: Static objects blend into the background, while moving ones draw the eye. A cup spilling tea is easier to recall than a cup on a table.
Pick a verb that shows what happens to the item, such as crack, spin or bounce. The verb turns a noun into a small story.
Make the movement larger than life, like a kettle shooting steam to the ceiling. Exaggeration sharpens the scene in your mind.

fig.title: Still to moving
fig.note: Movement turns a static cup into a scene.

ex.q: Which image is strongest for remembering eggs?
o: A cracked egg dripping onto the floor
A row of eggs on a shelf
ex.why: The cracked egg shows action and drama, so it stands out more than static eggs.

lessons.tip: Ask yourself what the item is doing right now.

quiz.q: Why add motion to an image?
o: It draws the eye and sticks better
It is required by the route
It makes the image take longer
quiz.why: Movement grabs attention, which helps the image store more strongly.

quiz.q: Which verb works best for a kettle?
quiz.why: Boils over is an action, so it creates a clear moment to remember.

lessons.t: Using size and colour for emphasis
lessons.intro: You will learn how size and colour can make the key part of an image stand out. Used sparingly, these changes help the important detail win attention.

cards.b: Make the key item larger than the others in the scene. A giant loaf on the table will stand out from ordinary bread.
A bright red bucket stands out from a grey room. Choose one strong colour so the emphasis is clear.
Too many emphasis tricks cancel each other out. One or two changes per item keep the scene simple.

fig.title: Changes per item
fig.note: Two emphasis changes is usually enough.

ex.q: You have 4 items. Each item has 2 emphasised features. How many emphasised features are there in total?
ex.why: Four items with two features each give 4 x 2 = 8 emphasised features.

lessons.tip: Make one thing bigger or brighter, not both at once, unless it is key.

quiz.q: What is a good use of size?
o: Making the key item larger than others
quiz.why: Size contrast makes the key item stand out in the scene.

quiz.q: How many emphasis changes are usually enough?
quiz.why: One or two changes keep emphasis clear rather than crowded.

lessons.t: Linking items with a clear story
lessons.intro: You will learn how to join items together with a short story. A story gives each item a cue for the next one, which makes a list easier to hold.

cards.b: A short story connects items so each one cues the next. Your brain remembers narratives more easily than random lists.
Pick a single action that links two neighbouring items, such as a hat falling into a bucket. One clear link is easier than a chain of unrelated ideas.
Two or three items in a scene is enough for a clear link. Long sagas take longer to rebuild when you recall them.

fig.title: Building a linked story
fig.note: Two items joined by one action make one link.

ex.q: A story links 3 items with one action between each pair of neighbours. How many links are in the story?
ex.why: Three items form two pairs of neighbours, so the story has 2 links.

lessons.tip: Say the story aloud once, then picture it.

quiz.q: Why does a story help recall?
o: It links items in a sequence
It removes the need for places
quiz.why: Stories chain items together so each one cues the next.

quiz.q: How many items suit one short story?
quiz.why: Two or three items fit a clear scene without overload.

lessons.t: Adding senses to your images
lessons.intro: You will learn how sound, smell and touch make an image feel real. Adding one or two senses gives the picture depth without crowding it.

cards.b: Images with sound, smell or touch feel more real. A sizzling pan is easier to recall than a plain frying pan.
Pick the sense that suits the item best, such as the smell of coffee. One strong sense is clearer than many weak ones.
Describe a specific sound, like a sharp crack, rather than a vague noise. Specific sensations anchor items more firmly.

fig.title: Senses in one image
fig.note: Use two or three senses per image.

ex.q: An image uses 2 senses for each of 5 items. How many sensory details are there in total?
ex.why: Each of the 5 items has 2 senses, so 5 x 2 = 10 sensory details.

lessons.tip: Add one smell or sound to the scene whenever you can.

quiz.q: What do sensory details do for an image?
o: Make it more real and memorable
quiz.why: Several senses make the scene feel real, which helps it stick.

quiz.q: How many senses are suggested per image?
quiz.why: Two or three senses give depth without crowding the picture.

lessons.t: Sound-alike cues for hard words
lessons.intro: You will learn how to use a word that sounds like something you can picture. Sound-alike cues make names and unfamiliar words much easier to hold.

cards.b: Many words sound like an object you can picture. A name like Lyon can be linked to a lion.
Once you hear the sound-alike, place the object in your palace. Put the lion on the sofa so the name comes back with the place.
Simple, obvious sound links work best. Long or clever twists slow recall because you must decode them first.

fig.title: Sound-alike cue versus label
fig.note: Sound-alike cues help with names and hard words.

ex.q: You need to remember the word pair. Which sound-alike cue is best?
ex.why: Pear sounds like pair, so the fruit gives an instant link to the word.

lessons.tip: Say the word aloud to find a clear sound link.

quiz.q: What do sound-alike cues help you remember?
quiz.why: Sound links turn an unfamiliar word into a familiar object.

quiz.q: Which cue is best for Lyon?
quiz.why: A lion matches the sound of Lyon, which makes the link instant.

lessons.t: Making people and names memorable
lessons.intro: You will learn how to attach a name and a face to a single spot in your palace. A clear visual feature gives the name something to hang on.

cards.b: People are hard to recall unless you tie them to a clear feature. A bright scarf or a large hat gives you a visual hook.

cards.h: Turn the name into a picture
cards.b: Use the sound-alike method to convert the name into an object. Pair the object with the feature so both are remembered together.

cards.h: Place the pair in a fixed spot
cards.b: Put the person and their name on one landmark in your palace. The place then reminds you of both the face and the name.

fig.title: Name and face loop
fig.note: Work through the loop for each new person.

ex.q: You meet 4 people and give each one a name cue plus one visual feature. How many separate cues do you create?
ex.why: Each person needs two cues, a name cue and a feature, so 4 x 2 = 8 cues.

lessons.tip: Repeat the name once in conversation to lock it in.

quiz.q: What makes a face easier to recall?
quiz.why: A distinct feature gives your memory a visual hook to hang the name on.

quiz.q: Where should the person and their name go?
o: In the middle of a hallway
quiz.why: A fixed landmark keeps the pair together so the place reminds you of both.

lessons.t: Combining image and place in one scene
lessons.intro: You will learn how to join an image to a specific landmark in one scene. The landmark then becomes the cue that brings the image back.

cards.h: Anchor the image to the spot
cards.b: Place the image on the exact landmark rather than near it. The landmark then becomes the cue that brings the image back.
Describe where the item sits, what it touches and what it does. A milk carton spilling over the sink is more precise than a carton somewhere.

cards.h: Keep the scene in one place
cards.b: Stay in the same location for the full picture rather than jumping around. One scene per spot keeps the route orderly.

fig.title: One scene per spot
fig.note: Each scene uses one place and one item.

ex.q: A landmark holds 1 image. Your route has 7 landmarks, and you want 3 images on each. How many images in total?
ex.why: Seven landmarks with three images each gives 7 x 3 = 21 images.

lessons.tip: Picture the item touching the landmark, not hovering near it.

quiz.q: Why put the image on the exact landmark?
o: The landmark becomes the cue for the image
It saves room on the route
quiz.why: A precise anchor makes the landmark bring the image back on recall.

quiz.q: What makes a scene specific?
o: Describing where the item sits and what it does
quiz.why: Specific positions and actions give the scene detail that memory can grip.

lessons.t: Reviewing images before placing them
lessons.intro: You will learn how to check each image before you place it in your palace. A quick review stops weak images from entering your route.

cards.h: Check the image before you place it
cards.b: Picture the item once more and confirm it is clear and vivid. A quick check stops weak images from going into your palace.
Make sure the new image does not blend into a neighbour. Two similar images in one spot cause confusion later.
Spend only a few seconds on each item. Long reviews slow your progress without making the image much stronger.

fig.title: Seconds per item
fig.note: Seconds spent on each item, about four in total.

ex.q: You prepare 12 items, each needing 4 seconds of imagining, checking and placing. How many seconds in total?
ex.why: Each item takes 4 seconds, so 12 x 4 = 48 seconds in total.

lessons.tip: If you cannot see the image clearly, change it now.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of reviewing an image?
o: To confirm it is clear and vivid
quiz.why: A clear image is easier to recall, so checking first saves trouble later.

quiz.q: Why avoid similar images in one spot?
quiz.why: Similar images placed together compete, making each harder to separate.

lessons.t: Chunking a long list into groups
lessons.intro: You will learn how to split a long list into small groups before you memorise it. Groups make a big list feel manageable and easier to recall in order.

cards.h: Groups of three to five work
cards.b: Your memory handles small clusters more easily than one long string. Splitting a list into groups of three to five keeps each cluster manageable.

cards.h: Give each group its own area
cards.b: Assign one room or area to each group of items. The area becomes a boundary, so you know where one group stops.
Walk the first group, then the next, rather than scanning the whole list. Group-by-group recall keeps the order clear.

fig.title: Chunking a list
fig.note: Groups of three to five suit most people.

ex.q: You have 15 items and split them into groups of 5. How many groups are there?
ex.why: Fifteen divided by five gives 3 groups of 5 items each.

lessons.tip: Count the groups before you start placing items.

quiz.q: What size of group suits most people?
quiz.why: Small clusters are easier to hold, so three to five is a practical size.

quiz.q: Why assign each group an area?
o: To mark where one group stops
quiz.why: A clear boundary tells you where each group begins and ends.

lessons.t: Two buildings in one palace
lessons.intro: You will learn how to extend a palace across two buildings when one is not big enough. A clear transition keeps the longer route easy to follow.

cards.h: Use a second building for overflow
cards.b: When one building runs out of spots, continue the route in a second building. Keep the transition clear with a fixed doorway between them.
Use a distinct gate or door where you switch buildings. The change tells you the route has moved on.

cards.h: Keep the walking rule the same
cards.b: Use the same direction and pace in every building. Consistent rules make the extended palace feel like one route.

fig.title: Two buildings, one route
fig.note: The gate marks the move into a second building.

ex.q: Building A has 12 spots and building B has 9 spots. You fill each spot with 2 items. How many items are there in total?
ex.why: Together the buildings have 12 + 9 = 21 spots, and 21 x 2 = 42 items.

lessons.tip: Walk through the transition gate at least once in your head.

quiz.q: What marks the move to a second building?
quiz.why: A clear threshold signals that the route has moved on.

quiz.q: Which rule should stay the same across buildings?
quiz.why: Consistent rules make the extended route feel like one continuous walk.

lessons.t: Numbering items with a peg system
lessons.intro: You will learn how a peg system gives each number a fixed hook for an item. With pegs, you can jump straight to any numbered item without walking the whole list.

cards.b: A peg is a memorised object for each number, such as a bun for one. Once learned, the pegs never change and act as hooks.

cards.h: Hang each item on its peg
cards.b: For item number three, picture the item hanging on the tree, your peg for three. The number and the item are then linked in one scene.
Because each number has a fixed hook, you can recall item fourteen without walking the whole list. This is the main benefit of pegs.

fig.title: Peg system versus plain list
fig.note: Pegs let you jump straight to any numbered item.

ex.q: Your peg list gives number 4 as a door. Item 4 on your list is a cup. Which picture links them?
ex.why: Peg four is a door, so the cup is pictured on the door to link item four to its peg.

lessons.tip: Learn the peg list until you can say it in any order.

quiz.q: What is a peg in this system?
o: A fixed object for each number
quiz.why: Each number is paired with a memorised object that serves as its hook.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of pegs?
o: Jumping to any numbered item directly
quiz.why: Each number has its own hook, so you can reach any item without walking through all of them.

lessons.t: Learning the first five pegs
lessons.intro: You will learn the first five pegs of a common peg system. Learning them well is the foundation for pegging any longer list.

cards.b: Rhymes make pegs easier to learn, as in one is a bun and two is a shoe. The rhyme gives you a sound cue for each number.
Picture each peg object clearly, such as a shoe you could touch. A vivid peg is easier to hang items on.
Say the pegs aloud in sequence, then backwards. Reversal practice shows whether you know each peg by heart.

fig.title: The first five pegs
fig.note: Learn the first five pegs before the rest.

ex.q: Peg 2 is a shoe and peg 5 is a hive. How many numbers lie strictly between 2 and 5?
ex.why: The numbers between them are 3 and 4, so there are 2 numbers.

lessons.tip: Test yourself by naming the peg for any number in random order.

quiz.q: What helps a peg list stick?
quiz.why: Rhymes give a sound cue, which makes each number-object pair easier to recall.

quiz.q: How should you practise the pegs?
o: Say them in order and backwards
quiz.why: Reversal practice confirms you know each peg, not just the order.

lessons.t: Memorising a shopping list of twenty
lessons.intro: You will learn how to memorise a list of twenty items by pairing each one with a peg. Pairing each item with its number keeps the whole list in order.

cards.h: Pair each item with a peg
cards.b: Take the first item and hang it on peg one, the bun. Work through the list in order so every item has its own number.

cards.h: Use the peg for each number
cards.b: For number two, picture the item on a shoe, your peg for two. The peg tells you which item to recall.
A single strong picture per item works best for a long list. Overloaded scenes slow recall when you need many items quickly.

fig.title: Numbered shopping items
fig.note: Each number pairs with one item.

ex.q: A list has 20 items, and you pair them with pegs 1 to 20. You recall 17 correctly. How many did you miss?
ex.why: Twenty items minus seventeen recalled leaves 3 missed items.

lessons.tip: Recall one item, then pause before moving to the next.

quiz.q: What does each peg do in a numbered list?
quiz.why: Each peg is a fixed hook for one number and its item.

quiz.q: Why keep scenes simple for a long list?
quiz.why: Heavy scenes take longer to decode, which slows you down across many items.

lessons.t: Using a second palace for overflow
lessons.intro: You will learn how to split a long list across two palaces. Choosing a second palace early keeps your routes separate and your workload steady.

cards.b: Give each palace its own name, route and starting point. Clear separation stops items drifting between the two routes.
Do not wait until the first palace is full before choosing a second one. Planning ahead keeps the workload steady.
Before you start recalling, decide which palace holds the list. Naming it first prevents searching the wrong route.

fig.title: Spots across two palaces
fig.note: Two palaces of ten spots each cover twenty items.

ex.q: You have 27 items. Palace A holds 10 items and palace B holds 10 items. How many items still need a place?
ex.why: Ten plus ten is 20, so 27 minus 20 leaves 7 items that still need a place.

lessons.tip: Name each palace with a simple label you can say quickly.

quiz.q: Why keep palaces separate?
o: It stops items drifting between routes
It removes the need to walk
quiz.why: Distinct routes keep items where they belong.

quiz.q: When should you start a second palace?
o: After the first one is ruined
Before the first palace is full
quiz.why: Planning ahead avoids crowding and keeps your workload steady.

lessons.t: Recalling a list in reverse order
lessons.intro: You will learn how to recall a list backwards from its last item. Reverse recall is a strong check that you know each spot and not just the sequence.

cards.b: Walking backwards shows whether you truly know each spot, not just the sequence. It is a strong check of your memory.
Jump to the final landmark and work toward the first. Starting at the end forces you to recall each item from its own place.
Keep count as you recall so you know when you are finished. A count stops you stopping early or going on forever.

fig.title: Reverse recall
fig.note: Reverse recall is a good finishing check.

ex.q: A list has 12 items. You recall in reverse and stop after 9. How many items are still missing?
ex.why: Twelve minus nine equals 3 items still missing.

lessons.tip: Use reverse recall as a finishing check on every long list.

quiz.q: What does reverse recall test?
o: Whether you know each spot, not just the order
quiz.why: Reverse recall reveals knowledge of each place independently of the sequence.

quiz.q: Why count while you recall?
o: To know when the list is finished
quiz.why: A count tells you whether you have reached every item.

lessons.t: Memorising a string of digits
lessons.intro: You will learn how to memorise a long string of digits by grouping them. Turning each group into a picture makes the digits far easier to hold in order.

cards.b: A long run of digits is easier to hold as groups of three. Each group becomes one unit you can picture and recall.
Turn each three-digit group into a single scene, such as three cups stacked on a shelf. Pictures make the group stable in your palace.
Place each group on the next landmark in your route. The route then keeps the groups in order automatically.

fig.title: Nine digits in a grid
fig.note: A 3 by 3 grid holds nine digits, chunked by row.

ex.q: A string of 9 digits is split into groups of 3. How many groups are there?
ex.why: Nine digits in groups of three make 9 divided by 3, which is 3 groups.

lessons.tip: Say the digits in groups, never as one long run.

quiz.q: Why chunk digits into groups of three?
o: Longer runs are easier to hold
Groups become units you can picture
Groups stop the route from moving
quiz.why: Each group becomes one picture, which is much easier to recall than single digits.

quiz.q: Where should each group go?
o: On the next landmark in the route
On the same landmark every time
quiz.why: Consecutive landmarks keep the groups in order without extra effort.

lessons.t: Cramming versus spaced review
lessons.intro: You will learn why spreading your reviews over several days works better than one long session. Spaced review keeps your palace strong for weeks.

cards.b: Revisit the palace after one day, then after a week. Gaps between reviews make your memory rebuild the route, which strengthens it.
Ten minutes of walking is usually better than one long session. Short sessions keep attention high and prevent fatigue.
Recall the list first, then check your notes. Testing yourself is one of the strongest forms of review.

fig.title: Cramming versus spaced review
fig.note: Review a palace after a day, then again after a week.

ex.q: You review a palace on day 1, day 3 and day 7. How many days pass between the first and last review?
ex.why: From day 1 to day 7 is 7 minus 1, which is 6 days.

lessons.tip: Review as soon as you feel you are about to forget.

quiz.q: What is spaced review?
quiz.why: Spacing reviews out makes your memory work harder, which builds stronger recall.

quiz.q: What is the best way to review?
quiz.why: Active recall strengthens memory more than rereading does.

lessons.t: Putting it together for thirty items
lessons.intro: You will learn how to combine every technique to remember a list of thirty items. Planning spots, pictures, pegs and review together makes a long list manageable.

cards.b: Choose a route with at least thirty spots, or plan a second palace. Counting spots in advance means every item has a home.
Use vivid pictures, pegs for numbers and sound-alike cues for names. Each technique covers a weakness of the others.
Walk the route, name every item, then check against your list. Your score tells you which spots need more work.

fig.title: The full method
fig.note: Repeat the loop until the whole list is secure.

ex.q: You want to remember 30 items. Your route has 4 rooms with 6 spots each. Are there enough spots?
ex.why: Four rooms of six spots give 4 x 6 = 24 spots, which is 6 short of 30, so a second palace is needed.

lessons.tip: Plan your spots before your items so the route never runs out.

quiz.q: What if a route has fewer spots than items?
quiz.why: A second palace gives extra spots so no items are left without a home.

quiz.q: Which technique helps with numbered lists?
quiz.why: Pegs give each number a fixed hook, which suits numbered recall.
